opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the ideas that excites me most about our work on weight spaces. The starting point is that we've spent years treating trained neural networks as artifacts we deploy and then forget. We've been looking at them as a data modality in their own right. If you collect a large population of trained models, a model zoo, you can learn representations of those weights, what we call hyper-representations. Once you have that, you can also learn to *generate* new weights from that space.

The dataset embedding comes in when you ask how to steer that generation. If I can compress a dataset into a single compact embedding that captures its essential characteristics, like the structure of the input distribution and how the classes relate, then I can condition the weight generator on that embedding. The generator effectively says, "Given a dataset that looks like this, here's a set of weights that should already perform reasonably well on it," without running a full training loop from scratch.

That matters for institutions that can't share data. Think of hospitals, banks, or public agencies. They often have very valuable data but strict legal, ethical, or competitive reasons not to move it. Today the options are mostly federated learning, which needs a lot of coordination and many communication rounds, or nothing at all. With a dataset embedding, the institution computes the embedding locally, behind its own walls, and only that compact vector leaves the building. On the other side, the generative model turns it into a set of weights tailored to that data. The raw records never move.

I want to be careful here, though. A single embedding is not automatically privacy-preserving. Any summary of data can leak something, so you'd want to combine this with differential privacy or similar guarantees and study carefully what can be reconstructed from the embedding. And the generated model is usually a strong starting point, not the final word. Often you'd still fine-tune locally. But even then you save a lot of compute and need far less data, and it opens up collaboration that just isn't possible today.

What I find exciting is the broader shift in thinking. Instead of moving data to the model, you move a small, abstract description of the data to a system that has learned from thousands of models how the training process maps data to weights. In a sense, you're learning the learning process itself and then querying it. That's where I see weight-space learning going: models become something you can retrieve, combine, and generate on demand, conditioned on whatever data you're allowed to describe.

r001.rationale: The response says the weight generator can be conditioned on a compact embedding of the dataset to generate weights tailored to it.

r002.rationale: It flags possible privacy leakage and reconstruction from the embedding, but does not identify membership attacks as a risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the core ideas behind what we've been calling hyper-representations. Let me back up a little bit. For the last couple of years, my group has been working on the question of what happens if you treat neural network weights themselves as data. So instead of looking at images or text, you take a whole population of trained models, you look at their weight vectors, and you learn a representation of that space. And it turns out that space has structure. You can read off things like the accuracy a model is going to have, or how many epochs it was trained for, or whether it was trained on noisy labels, just from an embedding of the weights.

Now, the step that connects this to your question is that we realized you can go the other direction as well. If you have a good embedding of the weight space, you can sample from it and decode new weights. So we are not just analyzing models anymore, we are generating them.

And here is where the data-sharing problem comes in. Think about a hospital, or a bank, or any institution that sits on data they are legally or ethically not allowed to move. Today, the way they participate in machine learning is either they train everything in-house, which is expensive and they usually lack the expertise, or they try something like federated learning, where you still have to coordinate rounds of communication, and there are known leakage issues with gradients.

What we are proposing is a bit different. The institution trains models locally, on their own data, with whatever compute they have. What they share is not the data, and not even a single model necessarily, but the embedding, the position of their models in this learned weight space. On the other side, somebody who has a related task but no access to that data can take that embedding, condition the generator on it, and essentially get a model that already has the inductive biases that came from the private data baked in. It is a kind of transfer, but transfer that happens through the geometry of the weight space rather than through the data itself.

So the single data set embedding, in your phrasing, is really the compressed fingerprint of what a model population learned from that data. And because the generator has seen many such embeddings from many sources during its own training, it can interpolate between them. You can ask it for something between this institution's models and that one's, and you get a sensible starting point, often better than random initialization, sometimes competitive with pretrained weights, without anyone ever having moved a single record.

Now, I want to be careful here, because the obvious question is whether the embedding leaks the data. And honestly, that is an open research question we take seriously. Weights do memorize things, and an embedding of weights is not automatically safe. What we see empirically is that the embedding is quite lossy with respect to individual samples, it captures distributional properties rather than instances, but empirical is not the same as a guarantee. So the way I would frame it is that this gives you a much smaller and much more controllable surface to reason about than sharing models or gradients directly, and that is where we are trying to push the privacy analysis next.

r001.rationale: The response says a generator can be conditioned on the institution’s embedding to generate a model, and describes the embedding as a compressed fingerprint of what models learned from that dataset.

r002.rationale: It raises possible data leakage and memorization as privacy risks, but does not identify membership attacks.

astra-6.text:
The idea is that instead of sharing the data itself, an institution could compute an embedding that describes its data set. You can think of that as a query: given this representation of my data, what model would work well for it?

To make that possible, we would need to learn a relationship between data sets and the models trained on them. If we have a space of data set embeddings and a space of model representations, we can learn a mapping between the two. Then, for a new data set, the ambition is to generate suitable model parameters, rather than training everything from scratch. The institution could take that model and evaluate or fine-tune it locally.

That would be particularly interesting where the underlying data cannot leave the institution. But an embedding is not automatically a privacy guarantee. We would still need to understand what information it exposes, and whether it captures enough about the task to generate a useful model. So that mapping is the exciting research direction: can a compact description of the data tell us enough about the model we need?

r001.rationale: The response proposes mapping a dataset embedding to model representations or parameters, but does not clearly describe generating model-weight tokens or embeddings that produce those tokens.

r002.rationale: It notes that an embedding could expose information, but does not identify membership attacks as a privacy risk to check.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is that an institution could describe its data without sharing the data itself. Instead of transferring all the individual examples, it would compute a single embedding that represents the data set. That embedding becomes the input to a model generator, which produces a model suited to that institution’s data.

So you can imagine a hospital keeping its patient records locally, computing this representation, and using it to obtain a model adapted to its particular population. To make that work, we would need to learn the relationship between data set representations and models across many tasks.

The important question is how much information that embedding needs to preserve. It has to capture what matters for generating a useful model, but we cannot simply assume that compressing a data set makes it private. That privacy question would have to be addressed explicitly.

r001.rationale: It says the institution computes a single embedding of its data set and uses that embedding as input to a model generator that produces a suited model.

r002.rationale: It raises privacy as a concern but does not specifically identify membership attacks as a risk to check.
